tests.topic: The newspaper kiosk (edicola) at the corner of a street: what it sells besides newspapers (sticker packs, bus tickets, comics), when it opens, and why a boy stops there every Thursday.
A winter Sunday in a mountain house: the grandfather stirs polenta in a copper pot for forty minutes, pours it onto a wooden board, and cuts it with a thread instead of a knife.
Four cousins sleep at their grandparents' house for a week in July: mattresses on the floor of one room, the grandmother's rule of lights out at ten, and the whispering that goes on after.

A new boy joins a class in the middle of the year after moving from another city: on Monday he knows nobody and eats alone, the teacher seats him next to a talkative girl, and by Friday he plays at break.
Two siblings have ten euros to buy flowers for their mother at a flower stall: the roses cost too much, they disagree, and the florist suggests a small plant in a pot that lasts longer.
A country vet is called to a cowshed in the middle of the night because a calf is being born: the drive in the dark, the farmer waiting with a lamp, and the calf that stands up within an hour.
A girl is afraid of her vaccination at the clinic: the waiting room, the injection that is over in a second, the plaster with a drawing on it, and the fifteen minutes they must wait before leaving.
A "walking bus" to school: a line of children walks the same route every morning led by two parents in yellow vests, with fixed stops and times where others join.
The bell tower in the middle of a village: it rings every hour and can be heard from the fields, the children once climbed its narrow stairs, and from the top the houses look like toys.
Two friends tell each other what they want to be when they grow up, a vet and a pastry chef, and the reasons: one loves animals but is afraid of blood, the other already bakes with an uncle.
Fishermen find a sea turtle caught in a net and take it to a rescue centre: it is cared for over two months, and then children watch from the beach as it is set free and swims away.
A girl goes to a football stadium for the first time with her father: the climb up the stairs, the bright green of the pitch, the roar at the goal, and the team scarf she takes home.
A girl keeps a holiday diary: three lines every evening, a train ticket or a leaf glued on the page, the day she wrote nothing because it rained, and reading it again in winter.
A class measures a child's shadow in the schoolyard with chalk at nine, at noon and at three: it is long in the morning, shortest at noon, and points the other way in the afternoon.
Two children swap football stickers at break: one needs three to finish a page of the album, the other has many doubles, and they bargain over a rare shiny one.
A boy gets the shirt of his favourite football team with the number ten on the back and wants to wear it every day: his mother washes it at night, and one morning it is still wet.
A whole class learns the recorder for the music lesson: the squeaks of the first weeks, the neighbour who hears the practice at home, and the short tune they finally play together.
Street artists draw big pictures with coloured chalk on the pavement of a square: a girl watches one grow all afternoon, leaves a coin in the hat, and the rain washes it away at night.
How a child lived in ancient Rome: lessons at dawn writing on wax tablets, games with nuts instead of marbles, and a main meal eaten in the afternoon.
A grandmother and her grandson prepare an afternoon snack of bread, tomato, oil and salt instead of the packaged snack he asked for, and he is surprised at how good it is.
The rice fields of the northern plain: in spring they are flooded and look like a lake with white herons walking in it, in summer they turn green, and in autumn the rice is cut.
A village food festival for the strawberry harvest in June: volunteers cook in a big tent, people pay first and wait with a numbered ticket, and everyone eats at long shared tables.
A grandmother picks up her two grandchildren from school every day because the parents work until six: the walk home, the snack, the homework at her kitchen table.
The fifteen-minute morning break at a primary school: the snack eaten quickly, the games in the yard, the bell that always rings too soon, and what the class does instead on rainy days.
A brother and sister argue about whose turn it is to set the table and whose to clear it, check the list on the fridge, and find out that both were wrong.
A girl's first loose tooth: she wobbles it for a week, it falls out while she bites an apple, and in the morning she finds a coin under the pillow left by the little tooth mouse.
A family rides a cable car up a mountain in summer: the cabin hangs high above the trees, the children's ears pop, it is cold at the top even in August, and the cows below look like dots.
An old apartment building around a shared courtyard: the balconies run along the inside, neighbours talk from one to the other, and the children play below where no cars can enter.
On a Saturday in spring a class cleans a beach with gloves and bags: what they find most (bottle caps and plastic straws), the strangest object, and how many bags they fill by noon.
Two children on the way to school quiz each other on Italy's regions and their main cities before an oral test: one mixes up two cities and the other has a trick to remember them.

The old tale of the Befana, the old woman who flies on a broom on the night before the sixth of January: children hang up a stocking and find sweets, or a lump of black sugar "coal" if they were naughty.
A boy builds a small volcano of clay around a glass for the science fair and makes it "erupt" with vinegar, baking soda and red colouring; the first try at home floods the table.
In October a mother empties the wardrobe to put away summer clothes and take out winter ones: what no longer fits the boy, what goes to his younger cousin, and the jumper he refuses to give away.

A family goes to an opera on a summer night in an ancient open-air arena: the stone steps with rented cushions, the small candles lit by the audience, and the child who falls asleep in the second act.
A father and daughter at the pharmacy with a prescription: the pharmacist explains how many drops to take and when, and the girl asks why the green cross outside is blinking.
A class visits an art museum with a sheet of details to find in the paintings, a dog, a red hat, a lemon: which was hardest to find and which painting a boy liked most and why.
A class visits Pompeii, the Roman town buried by the volcano long ago: the stone streets with stepping stones to cross, a bakery with its oven, and a painted "beware of the dog" on a floor.
Lemons grown on narrow terraces on a steep coast above the sea: no machine can get there, so the crates are carried down the stone steps on shoulders, and the trees are covered against hail.
A small-town shop that closes from one to four in the afternoon: a visiting child arrives at two, finds the shutter down, and learns when to come back and why the owner goes home for lunch.
A grandfather and granddaughter get on a city bus: he shows her how to stamp the ticket in the machine, where to press the button for their stop, and why they give their seat to a woman with a baby.
A baker's day turned upside down: he starts work at two at night so the bread is warm at seven, sleeps after lunch, and sees his children only in the afternoon.
A girls' mini volleyball team loses every match in the autumn: the coach changes one thing in training, and in March they win for the first time, by two points.
A Sunday flea market where children sell their old toys and books on a blanket in the square: what a girl brought, what she sold first, what nobody wanted, and how much she earned.
A boy from the north on holiday in Sicily discovers the local summer breakfast, lemon crushed ice eaten with a soft sweet bun: he thinks ice in the morning is strange, then asks for it every day.
On a trip to Puglia a child asks a guide about the small white round houses with pointed stone roofs, the trulli: why the walls are so thick and why it is cool inside in August.
A family takes home a dog from the shelter: the rules they agree on (who walks him in the morning, who in the evening), his first night crying in the kitchen, and where he sleeps a week later.
A class trip by coach to a teaching farm: the children see how cheese is made from the morning milk, try to milk a goat, and eat their packed lunch on the grass.
The town police officer who stops the traffic in front of a school every morning with a whistle and a red paddle: he knows the children by name, and one week a stranger takes his place.
A boy falls from his bicycle and breaks his arm: the trip to the emergency room, the X-ray, a plaster cast for four weeks, and the classmates who all sign it.
A mother and son brushing teeth: she asks him to turn off the tap while he brushes, he does not see why, and she shows him with a bucket how much water runs away in two minutes.
Leaving for the holidays by car on the first Saturday of August: the long queue on the motorway, the stop at a service area for a sandwich, and arriving three hours later than planned.
The old bridge in Florence that has little shops built on both sides: what they sell, what you see through the opening in the middle, and why a visiting child thinks it is a street, not a bridge.
Swallows come back every spring to the same nest under a roof: the family watches them repair it with mud, counts the chicks, and one September morning the nest is empty.
A family's week in the mountains in February to ski: the boy's first lesson with an instructor, falling off the ski lift, and the hot chocolate at the hut at the end of the day.
Two children in a bookshop choose a book as a birthday present for a friend: one wants an adventure story, the other a book about animals, and the bookseller asks what the friend likes.
A weekly comic magazine with a famous mouse and duck arrives at the newsstand on a fixed day: a girl reads it the same afternoon, her father read it as a boy, and they keep the old issues in a box.
A family rule about screens: half an hour of tablet after homework and none at the table; the kitchen timer that rings, and what the boy does on the evening the tablet is broken.
A grandmother sews a carnival costume from an old curtain because the shop ones cost too much: the fittings, the mask made of cardboard, and the parade in the square with confetti.
A grandfather plays the accordion at every family wedding and feast: the heavy instrument on his knees, the old dance tunes, and the granddaughter he teaches to dance standing on his feet.
A girl finds an old telephone with a round dial in her grandfather's cellar and he explains how it worked: one phone for the whole family, fixed to the wall by a wire, and numbers learned by heart.

In a town known for its pottery a girl paints a plate in a workshop: the pale colours she puts on with a thin brush, the wait while it is fired in the kiln, and how bright they are when she collects it.
The stone roads the ancient Romans built: straight for many kilometres, with stones at the side to show the distance, and a class works out how many days a walker needed from Rome to the sea.
A shepherd takes his sheep up to the mountain pastures at the start of summer and down again in autumn: the two dogs, the days of walking, and the cheese he makes up there.
One day in August a whole family makes tomato sauce for the winter in the courtyard: washing crates of tomatoes, the big pot on the fire, filling the glass bottles, and counting them at the end.
A father takes his son to his own barber for the first time: the boy says how short he wants it, the barber raises the chair and puts on the cape, and the father is surprised by the result.
A family spends two weeks of August at the same beach every year: the rented umbrella in the third row, the rule about not swimming right after lunch, and the evening walk for ice cream.
The last day of school in June and the report card: a girl is proud of her mark in mathematics, less of the one in drawing, and what her parents say when they read it.
A lifeguard on a beach in summer: he sits on the high chair, raises a red flag when the sea is rough, and one afternoon whistles at two boys who swim out too far.
A school nurse explains why and when to wash hands: before eating, after the bathroom and after playing outside, for as long as it takes to count slowly to twenty.
After the open day at the music school two friends talk about which instrument to choose: one wants the drums but lives in a flat, the other likes the violin but found it hard to hold.
A night ferry crossing to Sardinia for the summer holiday: the car parked in the ship's belly, the small cabin with bunk beds, and the island appearing at breakfast time.
In Bologna long covered walkways run along the streets: a girl walks to school under them on a rainy day without opening her umbrella, and counts the columns on the way.
A sudden summer thunderstorm at the beach: the sky turns dark in a few minutes, everyone runs to close the umbrellas, it rains hard for half an hour, and then the sun returns.
The great bicycle race passes through a small town one day in May: people wait for hours along the road, the riders fly by in less than a minute, and a boy catches a water bottle.
Two classmates paint the sea for art class: one uses only blue, the other mixes green and grey because that is how she saw it in winter, and they compare the results.
A boy writes his letter to Father Christmas in early December: he may ask for three things, crosses one out and changes it, and adds a line asking for something for his little sister.
On a night around the tenth of August families lie on blankets in a dark field to watch shooting stars: how long they wait for the first, how many a girl counts, and the wish she keeps secret.
A boy gets all his clothes from an older cousin in a big bag twice a year: the jacket he loves, the trousers that are too long, and the one time he asks for something new of his own.

Once a year in February a family stays up late to watch the national song festival on television: each person gives marks on a sheet of paper, they argue, and the children fall asleep before the winner.
A grandmother tells her granddaughter what school was like when she was small: one teacher for forty children, ink and pen nibs, walking three kilometres, and a stove in the classroom.
A boy on holiday collects small stones of different colours on the beach and at home glues them on a board to make a fish, after seeing an ancient floor mosaic on a trip.
A grandmother shows her grandson a drawer of old lira coins and notes from before the euro: prices were in thousands, an ice cream cost "a thousand", and he thinks everyone was rich.
An orange grove in Sicily where the fruit is picked in winter, not summer: a family of growers, the red oranges inside, and the crates that travel north by lorry in two days.
The winter sales that start in January: a mother waits for them to buy a coat that cost too much in December, and what the price tag in the shop window shows before and after.
A girl asks a farmer at his market stall why there are no strawberries in December: he tells her what grows in each season on his land and what he sells today instead.
The big family lunch outdoors on the fifteenth of August, the Ferragosto holiday: the long table under the trees, the cold dishes each relative brings, and the watermelon kept cool in the fountain.
The family prepares a surprise for the grandfather's seventieth birthday: the children draw a card, the aunt hides the cake at the neighbour's, and the grandfather comes home earlier than expected.
A class builds its own small library on a shelf: every child brings one book from home, there is a notebook to write who borrows what, and one book that everybody wants.
A girl's mother drives a city bus: her shifts change every week, she knows the regular passengers by face, and once a month the girl rides the whole route sitting behind her.
A child and the owner of a stationery shop go through the teacher's list of things to buy before school starts: the squared notebooks are sold out, and there are two pencil cases at different prices.
A girl cannot read the blackboard from the last row: the eye test with letters that get smaller, the choice of the frame, and how the trees look when she first wears the glasses.
A girl learns to ride her bicycle without training wheels on the path of a park: her father holds the saddle, she falls twice, and she does not notice when he lets go.

A very old round temple in Rome has a great dome with an open hole in the middle: a child visits on a rainy day, sees the rain fall inside, and finds the small holes in the floor where the water runs away.
A town under the volcano Etna in Sicily: some mornings black sand from the volcano covers balconies and cars, people sweep it up like snow, and a girl explains why nobody there is frightened.
Two classmates read the school canteen menu for the week: which day has their favourite dish, which day has the fish they do not like, and what one of them will swap for fruit.
Old men play bocce on a gravel lane in the park every afternoon: a grandfather explains the game to his granddaughter, lets her throw the small ball, and her team wins by one point.
A class must learn a short rhyme about the months by heart for Monday: a girl repeats it in the bath, in the car and at dinner, forgets one line in class, and a friend whispers it.
After rain a boy sees a rainbow and his mother shows him how to make a small one in the garden with the hose, standing with the sun behind them; the order of the colours he notices.
A grandmother knits a scarf for each grandchild every winter and lets them choose the colour: one scarf comes out far too long, and how the girl wears it anyway.
A girl's weekly piano lesson with an old teacher in a flat full of clocks: ten minutes of scales first, the piece she must repeat slowly, and the sweet she gets at the end.
A family builds the Christmas nativity scene on a table on the eighth of December: moss from the wood, a mirror for the lake, paper mountains, and the baby figure added only on the last night.
An old neighbour tells children about the first television in the village: only the bar had one, everyone brought a chair on Thursday evening, and children watched from the window.
The wheat harvest in July: the big machine works in the field until late at night before the rain comes, the grain goes away by lorry, and the round bales of straw are left on the field.
A fishmonger at a seaside town market: he gets up before dawn to buy fish at the harbour, by noon the ice counter is almost empty, and the last fish is sold at a lower price.
On moving day two sisters see their new flat and decide who gets which bed in the shared room: both want the one by the window, and they find a rule that lets them take turns.
A boy leaves all his summer holiday homework for the last week of August, while his sister did two pages every morning in July: what the last days of holiday look like for each.

On the first day at the beach a boy refuses sun cream and by evening his shoulders are red and sore: the next day he stays under the umbrella in a T-shirt, and the family rule about the hours around noon.
A train strike on a Friday: a father who commutes cannot get to work the usual way, tries the bus, and ends up sharing a neighbour's car; what time he finally arrives.
In the southern town of Matera people once lived in houses dug into the rock: one room for the whole family and the animals too, cool in summer, and water collected from the rain.
One Sunday a month a city closes its centre to cars: children skate and cycle in the middle of the road, a boy notices how quiet it is, and at six in the evening the traffic comes back.
The family plays tombola on Christmas evening: the grandfather calls the numbers with funny names, the children cover them with beans, and the youngest wins the last prize.
The old fable of the cicada who sings all summer and the ant who stores food: what each does in the warm months, what happens when winter comes, and what the ant answers.
A simple kitchen experiment: a girl guesses which things will float in a bowl of water (an ice cube, a coin, a cork, an orange with and without peel) and is wrong about two of them.
A mountain trip in spring: the mother makes everyone dress "like an onion" in layers, the children complain in the morning cold, and by noon the jackets are tied around their waists.

For a school task a boy interviews his mother, a hospital nurse who works nights: at what time she leaves, what she does while the patients sleep, and why she has breakfast when he does and then goes to bed.
A children's choir rehearses for the Christmas concert in the church: where the small ones stand, the song that is too high for the boys, and the cold in the church that makes them sing with scarves.
A family watches a glassblower on the island of Murano near Venice: the glowing ball on the end of a long pipe, the breath that makes it grow, and the little horse he shapes in a minute.
The story of a boy from Venice who long ago travelled for years with his father and uncle to faraway China, saw things nobody at home believed, and told them in a book.
A beekeeper shows a class his hives at the edge of a field: the white suit and the smoke that calms the bees, the frames full of honey, and why he leaves some honey for the bees in winter.
At Christmas a family always buys two cakes because half of them like panettone with raisins and half like plain pandoro with sugar on top: who eats which, and what is left for breakfast.
